title: The Thief's Tale
summary: A reformed burglar in Cairo stood before the assembly of police captains to recount the turning point of his life:
full_text:
A reformed burglar in Cairo stood before the assembly of police captains to recount the turning point of his life:

'In my youth, I was a desperate pickpocket. One night, I broke into the house of the venerable Chief Judge Abu Tahir, intending to steal his gold. I found him sitting by a solitary candle, weeping as he prayed for the poor of the city.

When he heard my footstep, he did not cry out for the watchmen. He looked at me with deep, sorrowful eyes, poured me a cup of warm mint tea, and said:

"Brother, only desperate hunger could drive a strong young man to risk his life in the dark. Take this purse of twenty dinars; it was earned by my own labor. Go, buy tools, learn an honest craft, and remember that your Creator made your hands to build, not to plunder."

Those gentle words shattered the iron shell around my heart. I wept, kissed his hands, and renounced crime forever. I apprenticed myself to a brass-founder, and for twenty years have lived with clean hands, knowing that mercy is more powerful than all the gallows of the world.'
moral: A single act of judicial mercy and belief in human goodness can turn a thief into an upright citizen.
